cells.tense: Here, the building is done and the whole of it is standing, and you can see that.
cells.act: carry your own share, all of it
cells.ask: Pick the piece nearest finished and take the last stretch alone — no help called in. No clock on this one. When it's done, let it stand and don't reopen it.
cells.core:
There's a shape you've built, and you can see it whole now — not the parts, the shape itself, the way it holds. You finish what you start, and you finish it in a form that outlasts the mood you started it in. You can look at what you made and say what it's for without flinching, because it's simply true.

What keeps this honest is that you carry your own end of it. Pick the piece nearest finished and take the last stretch alone, no help called in, then let it stand and don't reopen it. No clock on this one — the finishing sets its own end. Something you finished will be asked what it's worth, and you'll know. The part nobody sees is that you rested before you finished — that's the strength this runs on, and it isn't a reward at the end.
cells.sheetLine: You finish what you start, and it stands.
cells.verb: carrying a form through to its standing finish
cells.place: where shape is read without its contents

cells.tense: The next version of this thing is already being sketched, and it has no floor under it yet.
cells.act: leave the heart open and empty a while
cells.ask: Sit beside something you've already finished, once a day for a week, and do nothing to it — no next version, no test, no fixing.
cells.core:
You've built things, and you're already sketching the next version — the one that fixes what this one couldn't, the one a year out, the one the plan is for. It isn't laziness. It's that you keep going past what's finished; whatever you just made gets stepped over on the way to what's next, and the form sitting there doesn't get counted.

There's another half to making things: letting one be finished. Sit beside something you've already finished, once a day for a week, and do nothing to it — no next version, no test, no fixing. Let the restlessness be there without acting on it. If the week ends and nothing new has been sketched, you'll know the difference between building and bracing. What you already made is allowed to be the last one for a while.
cells.sheetLine: You're already on the next version before this one is allowed to stand.
cells.verb: carrying a form through to its standing finish
cells.place: where shape is read without its contents

cells.tense: A door closed, and you're still holding the handle.
cells.act: describe what is in front of your eyes in five plain lines, no conclusions
cells.ask: Take whatever's nearest and write five plain lines about it — what it is, how it looks, no conclusions — then put the page away. No clock.
cells.core:
Where you build, nothing has been getting finished — there's a last step you don't take, or a thing you've stopped calling yours. It's done and behind you, and the handle is still in your hand, whatever it was. The pattern you're good at seeing has become a place to live instead of a thing to use, and the minutes keep going into it.

Go plain. Take whatever's nearest and write five lines about it — what it is, how it looks, no conclusions, nothing about what it's for. Then put the page away. The lines don't have to be good; they have to be true and finished. Left alone, this is one piece out of ten, and the other nine stand without you having to hold them. What you already built doesn't need the account kept open.
cells.sheetLine: You're still holding the handle of a door that's closed.

cells.tense: You're laying out a structure room by room and calling it just how you think.
cells.act: notice what is before your eyes before naming it
cells.ask: Before your next idea takes shape, wait ten seconds and notice something you can see, untouched and unnamed. Once this week, done.
cells.core:
You lay things out — the order of a build, the shape under a plan, the way one thing has to come before another — and if someone asked, you'd say you're only working through what's there. The structures you draw are good. What's missing is that you made them. You file your handiwork under the facts of the situation, and the situation doesn't mind, but the credit keeps going somewhere you can't collect it.

The fix is small and comes before any diagram: next time, wait ten seconds and notice something actually there — a plain sight, untouched, before it has a name or a use. It buys you nothing. That's the point. Seeing is already yours; the drawing comes after, and the drawing is yours too. You'll keep the structure either way, but you won't have to pretend it drew itself.
cells.sheetLine: The structures are yours. You call them just how you think.
